title: Billions Vanished From a State Fund. Then Came the Parties, the Jets and a Superyacht
central_question: Where did the 1MDB money go, according to US prosecutors?
content_notes: Low Taek Jho has NOT been tried or convicted, is a fugitive whose whereabouts are not officially confirmed, and denies wrongdoing: every allegation is attributed (US prosecutors / the US Justice Department), the settlement is stated with 'admitting no guilt', and his denial is narrated and shown on a card. He appears only as an anonymous rim-lit silhouette (not a likeness), never handling money, never in a dock or cell. No celebrity is named or depicted; party guests are anonymous silhouettes. The film is named only as attributed to the Justice Department (and the Red Granite settlement). Najib Razak, Roger Ng and Tim Leissner appear only as typed names on a card, never drawn. The yacht, jet, mansion and harbour are generic drawings: no names, flags, logos, liveries or registration numbers; police uniforms carry no insignia. No real document, court material, banknote or photograph is imitated. Legal status verified 2026-10-12.

lines.text: US prosecutors say over $4.5 billion was siphoned from a Malaysian state fund.
And some of it, they say, bought a superyacht.
The fund was 1MDB. Prosecutors put financier Jho Low at its centre.
They say the money paid for a private jet,
lavish parties, mansions, diamonds and a Van Gogh.
Even The Wolf of Wall Street, the Justice Department says.
In 2018, at US request, Indonesia seized the superyacht in Bali.
In 2019 Low gave up over $700 million in assets, admitting no guilt.
Others were convicted, including a former prime minister.
Low has never been tried, and he denies wrongdoing.
Billions, prosecutors say. And one superyacht.

claims.text: The US Justice Department said high-level 1MDB officials and associates, including Low Taek Jho, siphoned more than $4.5 billion from Malaysia's state fund 1MDB (2009-2015). Attributed on screen and in narration to US prosecutors.

US prosecutors alleged that the superyacht Equanimity (about $250 million, per DOJ officials in 2017) was bought with money misappropriated from 1MDB. The yacht on screen is a generic drawing, not a replica.
1MDB (1Malaysia Development Berhad) is a Malaysian state fund; the DOJ describes it as a sovereign wealth fund.

US prosecutors place financier Low Taek Jho ('Jho Low') at the centre of the alleged scheme: he faces criminal charges in the US and Malaysia, is described as wanted for a leading role, and denies wrongdoing.

The DOJ alleged Low bought a Bombardier Global 5000 private jet for $35.4 million (2010) with misappropriated 1MDB funds; its 2016 actions sought 17 assets including a jet. The jet on screen is generic (no make, livery or registration).

Prosecution evidence at the 2022 Ng trial described lavish Las Vegas parties hosted by Low (including invoices of about $3.6 million for one party); the DOJ said he gambled away millions in allegedly misappropriated funds. No celebrity is named or depicted.
DOJ forfeiture actions targeted luxury real estate, art (including works by Van Gogh and Monet) and diamond jewellery allegedly bought with 1MDB funds.
The DOJ (Attorney General Lynch, July 2016) said associates allegedly used 1MDB proceeds to help fund the production of The Wolf of Wall Street. Attributed to the Justice Department.
Red Granite Pictures, the film's producer, agreed in March 2018 to pay the US government $60 million to settle the civil forfeiture suit, without admitting wrongdoing. On screen only.
On 28 February 2018 Indonesian police, at the request of US authorities (with the FBI), seized the Equanimity at Benoa, Bali. Low was not on board.
After the yacht was handed to Malaysia (2018), Malaysia sold it in April 2019 to Genting for $126 million.

In October 2019 Low and his family settled the US civil forfeiture cases (13 cases; assets in the US, UK and Switzerland worth more than $700 million). The settlement is not an admission of guilt or liability and does not resolve the criminal charges.

Former prime minister Najib Razak was convicted in the SRC International case (July 2020; 12 years, later halved by a pardons board) and, on 26 December 2025, in the main 1MDB trial (4 abuse-of-power and 21 money-laundering counts; 15 years). He denies wrongdoing; his lawyer said he would appeal.

Former Goldman banker Roger Ng was convicted by a Brooklyn jury in April 2022 (10 years, March 2023); Tim Leissner pleaded guilty in 2018 and was sentenced to 2 years in May 2025. On screen only. (Pras Michel, convicted 2023 and sentenced to 14 years in Nov 2025, is in the ledger but not on screen.)
Low has never been tried; he is a fugitive whose whereabouts are not officially confirmed (police still verifying claims in 2026) and he denies wrongdoing.
